Theorem 3 gives cheap collisions and a bridge-amplified multicollision: one inner collision and one connector yield equal-length Joux-style 2^k-multicollisions for every k, instead of Joux's k collision searches. Building on paths to a given inner state, Theorem 4 uses k bridges on the same capacity value x to give k^L full-state multicollisions of 2L+1 blocks after a prefix to x, for every L, at a fixed heuristic cost of E[T_k] ~ Gamma(k+1/2)/Gamma(k)*sqrt(2*2^c/q) with q=2p(1-p), about sqrt(4k)*2^(c/2) for balanced search (p=1/2), that does not depend on L; a binary Joux construction producing at least as many messages needs about ceil(L*log2(k)) collision searches, each of generic order 2^(c/2). Fixed-cost multicollisions were known for CubeHash, but they use the all-zero fixed state and their messages differ in length; to our knowledge, the k^L count of equal-length messages from k>1 bridges at an arbitrary x is new. It has no impact on SHA3-256. We give verified full-round examples on Keccak-f[200] and on Keccak-f[1600] with c=32, a full-round Keccak-f[1600] bridge with c=80, and a full-round c=80 example from the standard IV: an IV transition and three bridges (2^42.61 calls in total) give 3^3=27 distinct 1710-byte messages with a common digest.
The second part of the paper offers novel protocols built on the asymmetry between minting and forging Keccak bridges. They include proof of work with hardness-adaptive capacity, dual-capacity commitments anchored by the real SHA3-256 digest, bridges as zero-knowledge-committed tokens, and a self-enforcing bounty market for reduced-round security. To our knowledge, these are the first unkeyed Keccak-based protocols that deliberately set the capacity so that minting a generic bridge takes a feasible O(2^(c/2)) permutation calls, while the tunable hardness parameter c makes forging a bridge infeasible, since it requires O(2^c) permutation calls. We prove the four theorems, machine-check the stated algebraic results in Lean 4, and provide reproducible experiments and open-source proof-of-concept code. The applications are design proposals whose end-to-end security remains open.

item.title: Rerandomizable Garbling Beyond BHHO-KMHE and a Construction from LWE
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2664
Authors: Raphael Heitjohann, Jonas von der Heyden, Tibor Jager
Summary: Rerandomizable garbling schemes (RGS) are a fundamental primitive enabling advanced cryptographic constructions such as multi-hop homomorphic encryption (Gentry, Halevi, Vaikuntanathan, CRYPTO 2010), iO-combiners (Ananth, Jain, Naor, Sahai, Yogev, CRYPTO 2016), and YOSO-style MPC (Acharya, Hazay, Kolesnikov, Prabhakaran, TCC 2022 and CRYPTO 2024). All known RGS instantiations rely on discrete-logarithm-type assumptions, concretely via the BHHO scheme (Boneh, Halevi, Hamburg, Ostrovsky, CRYPTO 2008) and its recent pairing-based variant (Heitjohann, von der Heyden, Jager, CRYPTO 2025). This reliance stems from the use of key-and-message homomorphic encryption (KMHE) that supports rerandomization and strong "key-privacy under leakage", which hides the applied homomorphic transformations and is currently only achievable using BHHO-style bitwise encryption in combination with permutation-based homomorphisms.
Our first main contribution is a new garbling technique that shifts the burden of hiding homomorphic transformations from the encryption scheme to the garbling itself. This allows us to construct RGS from KMHE schemes with substantially weaker properties, avoiding the need for bitwise encryption and permutation-based homomorphisms, and enabling the construction of RGS from KMHE with other homomorphisms, such as additively-homomorphic ones.
As a second contribution, we give a concrete lattice-based instantiation of the required KMHE primitive, based on LWE. This construction is a variant of the GSW FHE scheme (Gentry, Sahai, Waters, CRYPTO 2013), which uses new techniques for rerandomization and is tailored to the requirements of our new garbling scheme by supporting a "homomorphic"/"lossy" mode. This yields the first RGS construction that does not rely on discrete-logarithm assumptions and may provide post-quantum security.

item.title: Quantum Multi-Collision Lower Bounds for Arbitrary Bounded Types
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2663
Authors: Tianci Peng, Shiqi Hou, Xiaoyang Dong
Summary: We study quantum collision finding for functions of prescribed exact type. For fixed constants $k\ge r\ge2$ and $N=kn$, consider functions $f:[N]\to\mathbb Z_q$ of type $(k^n)$, with exactly $n$ distinct output values and $k$ preimages for each value. We prove that the worst-case bounded-error quantum query complexity of finding $r$-collisions in $\ell$ distinct equality classes is \[ \Theta_{k,r}\!\left( \ell^{\,2^{r-1}/(2^r-1)} N^{(2^{r-1}-1)/(2^r-1)} \right) \] for $1\le\ell\le N^{2^{-r}}$. The result is uniform over all feasible alphabet sizes $q\ge n$.
Our proof uses the compressed permutation oracle (CPO). We establish a recurrence for intermediate collision counts and control its accumulated error to obtain database tails exponentially small in $\ell$. The improved CPO soundness estimate then converts these database bounds into function-query lower bounds.
Moreover, we extend the analysis to arbitrary exact types with bounded class sizes, without requiring any particular class size to occur linearly often. The resulting lower bounds are tight when forward permutation access is additionally available, although they need not be tight for the original function-query problem. Finally, a sampling reduction relates our collision bounds to sparse $k$-distinctness instances. A separate analysis using Belovs's transfer framework recovers the same lower-bound exponent, establishing a concrete connection between the two approaches.

item.title: Tractable, Not Truncated: Colored-Noise TRNG Security via Fractional Brownian Motion
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2662
Authors: Maciej Skórski, Nathalie Bochard, Licinius Benea
Summary: Oscillator-based true random number generators derive randomness from timing fluctuations driven by thermal and flicker noise, and flicker gains weight as technology advances and transistors shrink. Its long memory leaks information about past, which existing models either discard or truncate, overstating security.
We introduce a rigorous and tractable framework for colored noise, including the white and flicker noise of oscillators. We model the oscillator phase by fractional Brownian motion and prove a quasi-renewal property: the phase uncertainty left after conditioning on the entire past depends only on the elapsed time. This yields closed-form worst-case min-entropy and sampling requirements. We also extend spectral and Allan-variance analysis to finite samples, so the noise parameters are estimated consistently from a single timing trace. The pipeline from measurement to sampling requirement is closed-form and needs no simulation.
Experiments across FPGA and ASIC platforms show that flicker dominates: its variance meets white noise within about 100 cycles and accounts for more than 99% of uncertainty behind the targeted 0.99 min-entropy rate. Methods relying exclusively on thermal noise require adjustment or redesign: incorporating flicker noise enables a two-to-three orders of magnitude increase in bitrate.

item.title: Radical isogenies on every model
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2661
Authors: Thomas Decru
Summary: Radical isogeny formulae compute a cyclic chain of $N$-isogenies with one $N$th root per step and without sampling torsion points, but for general $N$ they were only known in Tate normal form. We give radical steps of every odd degree $N$ directly on short Weierstrass, Montgomery, twisted Edwards, Huff, extended Jacobi quartic, twisted Hessian, Legendre and Jacobi intersection curves, on Kummer lines, and on all curves with a rational point of order~$2$. Our approach is model-independent. The Tate normal form data is obtained from the $x$-coordinate of the kernel generator by a shifted recursion, and the codomain is recovered in the original model by locating the image of a distinguished torsion point, without square roots. In Tate normal form we lower the cost of a step from $12.5N$ to $10N$ multiplications plus one exponentiation, and short Weierstrass curves come close at $10N+35$. Montgomery and twisted Edwards curves cost $10.5N+O(1)$. However, pushing a point through their steps costs only $2N$ multiplications without precomputation, against $2N+16$ plus a shared $2N-7$ in Tate normal form, which makes them the cheapest models for chains that transport torsion points, e.g.\ for all $N\ge19$ when two points are pushed. The other models cost between $11.5N+O(\log N)$ and $15.5N+O(\log N)$ per step. All algorithms are inversion-free, with exact operation counts.

item.title: Towards Quantum Sensing for Side-Channel Analysis
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2660
Authors: Oliver Butowski, Paul Haas, Jonas Hasenkrug, Niklas Mathes, Emanuele Strieder, Michael Kunzer, Jan Jeske, Nisha Jacob Kabakci, Marc Stöttinger
Summary: Side-Channel Analysis is an established field of research to assess implementation vulnerabilities of cryptographic algorithms. One typically exploited side-channel is the electromagnetic (EM) near-field, which is proportional to the data-dependent currents flowing through an Integrated Circuit (IC). The field of Quantum Sensing (QS) based on Nitrogen-Vacancy (NV) centers has shown promising approaches for different measurement configurations like scanning or spatially resolved wide-field imaging. Already today, QS has been used in the analysis of (quasi-)static magnetic fields on ICs in spatially-resolved wide-field magnetometers. In this work, we study the applicability of QS for the analysis of dynamic EM fields of ICs. For the first time, we demonstrate spectral-temporal analysis of the EM-side-channel using an NV-center-based Radio-Frequency spectrometer. Our sensor has a real-time bandwidth of 1.1 GHz with adjustable center frequency and directly probes the frequency spectrum via NV center interactions in the time domain. The approach circumvents any computations like Fourier transforms or performing frequency sweeps, enabling GHz-realtime bandwidths. We use this spectrometer to analyze the EM emanations of an RSA decryption and perform leakage detection of a software implementation of the Number Theoretic Transform - a building block of all current lattice based post-quantum algorithms - running on a Cortex M4 commercial off-the-shelf microcontroller.

item.title: Alg\{Ossa\}: Decentralized Secure Aggregation with Rotating Committees and Eventual Delivery
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2659
Authors: Xiangyu Su, Yuma Tamagawa, Mario Larangeira, Zengpeng Li, Keisuke Tanaka
Summary: Secure aggregation lets clients reveal only an aggregate of their private contributions, supporting a variety of applications, including privacy-preserving sensing, collaborative analytics, and federated learning. Building on the single-server, committee-aided model for one-shot clients used by OPA and Willow~(CRYPTO~'25), we present Ossa, a generic construction with a modular security analysis. Ossa realizes the standard secure aggregation functionality with non-selective abort against a malicious server, but leaves role selection unspecified and provides no delivery guarantee. We therefore present AlgOssa, which integrates Ossa into an Algorand-style consensus backbone in which cryptographic sortition selects fresh potential leaders and verifier committees in each round and refreshes the decryptor committee from finalized chain state at key epochs. AlgOssa further selects the server from among the potential leaders, and we establish an explicit lower bound on the probability that the selected server is honest. Consequently, the probability that a round delivers a non-empty aggregate is bounded below by a positive constant, yielding an eventual delivery guarantee across repeated rounds. This variable delivery cadence fits delay-tolerant statistical sensing and, with persistent buffering and staleness control, buffered asynchronous federated learning. Our generic core supports classical and post-quantum instantiation routes; we evaluate complete local classical rounds and demonstrate the feasibility of the post-quantum route.

item.title: Unshuffling Fisher-Yates: Practical Recovery of Length-128 Permutations and Application to ML-DSA
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2658
Authors: Jonas Schupp, Anna Baumeister, Antonia Wachter-Zeh, Georg Sigl
Summary: Shuffling is a standard hiding countermeasure against (single-trace) side-channel attacks on the number-theoretic transform (NTT) of lattice-based post-quantum schemes, such as ML-DSA. The Fisher-Yates algorithm can be used to generate the underlying random permutation. Recovering this permutation itself from a single trace has so far only been studied for short sequences. We present a practical attack on a software implementation of Fisher-Yates for sequences of length 128, the number of butterfly operations in one layer of ML-DSA’s NTT. We identify the exploitable leakage of the algorithm, detect and remove the timing variations caused by rejection sampling and extract Hamming weight and identity leakage from a single trace per shuffle. We encode these hints as a constraint-programming problem with a soft objective function and enumerate the most likely permutations in order of descending likelihood. Applied to a shuffled ML-DSA-44 NTT, the recovered permutations are used to re-order the butterfly leakage, and recover the secret polynomial s1 either directly or up to a few coefficients that are enumerated directly. Protecting ML-DSA’s NTT with Fisher-Yates-based shuffling does, therefore, not, by itself, prevent side-channel-assisted key recovery.

item.title: Poly2MsgLeaks: Certified Key Recovery from Polynomial-to-Message Leakage
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2657
Authors: Yongseong Park, YoungChang Kim, Jeongdo Kim, Young-Sik Kim
Summary: We present Poly2MsgLeaks, a profiled chosen-ciphertext power-analysis attack that recovers the complete 512-coefficient public-key encryption (PKE) secret of SMAUG-T in its TiMER parameter set. Each polynomial-to-message (P2M) decision depends on four ternary secret coefficients and therefore on one of 81 local states. We characterize all admissible P2M predicates and show that our six-query schedule maps the 81 states to 57 binary transcripts; even with both exact polynomial weights, noiseless transcripts leave a mean residual ambiguity of 27.2 bits. Poly2MsgLeaks retains waveform scores for all 81 states, couples the 128 local blocks through the exact weights, and enumerates a calibrated cost region against the public-key relation. Under a uniform-matrix model, we prove that an incorrect key is released with probability at most $2^{-2095.6}$; for exchangeable calibration and evaluation keys, the probability that the true key lies outside the searched region is bounded without a channel model. Using six physical P2M traces recorded on an STM32F415, Poly2MsgLeaks recovers 999 of 1,000 previously unseen secrets, and a verifier-driven policy recovers all 1,000 secrets of a second cohort at a mean cost of 7.021 traces, without false acceptances. With the same decoder and limits, equalizing the scores within each transcript class reduces recovery from 998 to 112 keys. Against single-write message assembly and a two-share masked P2M, the evaluated six-execution attack recovers no complete secret.

item.title: Falcon Key Recovery from Joint Sampler Leakages
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2656
Authors: Youngchang Kim, Yongseong Park, Jaeho Jeon, Young-Sik Kim
Summary: Falcon and the forthcoming FN-DSA standard based on it generate signatures via discrete Gaussian sampling, during which power consumption leaks information about secret-dependent intermediate values. While prior attacks exploit sampler leakages individually or in pairs, we present a unified key-recovery framework that fuses three observations from each SamplerZ call: the signed-exponent class e(k) of the integer center, the random-sign bit b, and a multi-class proposal magnitude z0. These fused observations define magnitude-preserving intervals or rays for accepted sampler outputs. Leveraging an exact public linear relation that holds in the absence of modular wraparound, we map these candidate sets directly into slab and halfspace constraints on the secret key. The resulting system is solved via smooth softplus interval regression and bounded integer reconstruction with public-key validation, entirely bypassing computationally intensive lattice reductions such as LLL or BKZ. For PQClean Falcon-512 running at-O3 on an ARM Cortex-M4, our 17-class center classifier achieves 99.34% call-level accuracy on held-out test signatures from the profiling keys. The resulting attack recovers all 50 disjoint evaluation keys using at most 34 signatures (median 11), with a median post-classification key-recovery runtime of 17.54s per key. Furthermore, on c-fn-dsa, where center conversion relies on a single constant-time CLZ instruction, a reduced-resolution 7-class classifier combined with proposal leakage still recovers 38 of 50 keys within 200 signatures. These findings demonstrate that instruction-level normalization alone cannot prevent key recovery, underscoring that side-channel countermeasures for FN-DSA must protect all sampler leakage channels jointly.

item.title: OblivDGL: Oblivious Deep Graph Learning Made Practical
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2655
Authors: Yiming Qin, Xiaoning Liu, Shangqi Lai, Joseph K. Liu, Xingliang Yuan
Summary: The rapid deployment of Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) within Machine Learning as a Service (MLaaS) has opened up new privacy concerns. Both sensitive graph data and proprietary GNN models are submitted to and processed in third-party MLaaS platform for training and inference. To alleviate those concerns, recent efforts have been made to design tailored secure computation protocols for GNNs. Unfortunately, existing designs cannot accomplish security, functionality, and scalability simultaneously. They leak a certain degree of graph information, offer limited support on secure training of GNNs, and can hardly scale to large graphs.
In this paper, we design and implement OblivDGL, an oblivious deep graph learning framework for secure GNN inference and training. Our design is inspired by Deep Graph Library (DGL), an industrial practice for graph learning. At its core, we distill the secure computational patterns of GNNs into a generalized form, and empower both secure GNN training and inference through a novel oblivious message passing paradigm. To realize such a paradigm, we design a new oblivious graph representation, and realize it by function secret sharing (FSS), a lightweight secure computation technique with low latency. Compared to prior secure GNN systems, OblivDGL achieves the most stringent privacy guarantees, i.e., revealing no private information except for the total number of edges and nodes. One standout feature of OblivDGL is the scalability of processing encrypted graphs by carefully tailored parallelization designs. Extensive evaluations on four benchmark graph datasets demonstrate that, compared to state-of-the-art secure GNN frameworks, OblivDGL reduces communication cost by up to 1024x and achieves up to 14.3x speedup in runtime during secure training. For secure inference, OblivDGL achieves up to 754x lower communication and a 4.19x speedup.

item.title: When Algebraic Structure Meets Too Many Hints
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2654
Authors: Dongshu Cai, Yijian Liu, Xianhui Lu
Summary: The hint framework of Dachman-Soled, Ducas, Gong, and Rossi (CRYPTO 2020), together with the later too-many-hints analyses from May and Nowakowski (ASIACRYPT 2023) and Cao, Jiang, and Cheng (CRYPTO 2025), gives a classification of secret-dependent hints and LLL-breaking hint thresholds for LWE schemes. These values are now frequently adopted as the default benchmark for side-channel security evaluation. We show that applying them as a security metric is problematic.
DDGR categorizes hints based only on their local algebraic form, while the threshold analyses assume uniformly sampled hint vectors. Neither captures how the specific algebraic form of a hint governs the geometry of the resulting sparsified lattice. A hint’s class label and the corresponding uniform threshold therefore cannot, on their own, capture its real cryptanalytic power.
We illustrate this mismatch with two forms of structured leakage that naturally appear in ring and module lattice implementations, validated via synthetic experiments on Kyber-512. NTT-domain residues qualify formally as mod-$q$ hints, yet they recover the full Kyber-512 secret with roughly half as many hints as the uniform mod-$q$ bound predicts. Finite-precision FFT samples fall into the weaker approximate-hint class, and still only need $25\%$--$55\%$ of the hint budget required for uniform perfect hints.
The gap stems from algebraic structure: these hint families carry additional ring structure that enables tailored lattice recovery strategies, a distinction invisible under the uniform-sampling model.
We do not propose new attack optimizations. Our findings indicate that DDGR hint classes and too-many-hints thresholds are syntactic descriptions, not standalone security metrics for real leakage traces. Evaluating a side-channel leak requires considering the algebraic structure of the hint vectors, not just their category and quantity.

item.title: Analyzing Compiler-induced Constant-time Violations with Compiler at Scale
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2653
Authors: Jing Liu, Lucía Martínez Gavier, Zhiyuan Zhang, Marcel Böhme, Gilles Barthe
Summary: The constant-time programming policy is a de facto standard for cryptographic libraries to prevent timing side-channel attacks. However, compiler optimizations may break constant-time source code during compilation. Systematically preventing this requires understanding where a violation arises, how it is introduced, and which compiler configurations are problematic. Existing approaches analyze a single compilation point, either the final binary or one intermediate representation, and thus only partially answer the three questions.
We propose CTGREP, a compiler-based framework that answers all three questions by applying differential analysis across the entire compilation chain. We use CTGREP to analyze seven complete cryptographic libraries across three Clang versions, six target platforms, and thousands of compiler configurations. We systematically detect compiler-induced constant-time violations in the wild and collaborate with library developers to address 48 cases. We further identify seven new problematic LLVM passes, bypass and improve the state-of-the-art compiler-flag-based mitigation. Finally, we quantify how the compiler version, target platform, and optimization configuration affect the violations. By covering entire libraries across the full compilation chain, CTGREP effectively detects remaining compiler-induced constant-time violations and complements the community's ongoing hardening efforts.

item.title: Reverse Substitution in Secret Sharing: The Critical One-Half Threshold and a Route to Superpolynomial Lower Bounds
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2652
Authors: Shahram Khazaei
Summary: The contribution vector (convec) of a secret-sharing scheme is the vector of its normalized share sizes. The average and maximum coordinates of a convec give, respectively, the average and maximum information ratios of the scheme. Obtaining superlinear lower bounds on these quantities for unrestricted perfect secret sharing has remained a challenging open problem for about four decades.
In this paper, we study substitution, a natural way to build complicated access structures from simpler ones: one participant of an outer access structure is replaced by an inner access structure. Given secret-sharing schemes for the two factors, the standard forward construction composes them into a scheme for the composite access structure. We study the converse question. Given an arbitrary scheme for the composite access structure, we ask to what extent its convec admits a reverse factorization into convecs for the outer and inner factors, up to a common multiplicative loss.
Exact reversal is false: we give a counterexample whose optimal reverse factor is \(8/9\), with a composite scheme that is scalar-linear over every finite field. On the positive side, we prove that a factor \(1/2\) is always attainable, and that every fixed instance admits a strictly larger factor.
For a recursive family built from Csirmaz’s classical access structure \(\mathcal C_k\), whose distinguished set has size \(k\), we identify a critical reverse factor that determines when the resulting lower bound becomes superlinear. This critical factor exceeds one half by only an amount of order \((\log k)/k\). Crossing it yields superlinear lower bounds, while any fixed positive excess above one half gives a route to superpolynomial lower bounds. Using only Shannon inequalities, the corresponding recursive factor cannot cross the critical value. Thus any improvement sufficient to pass this threshold must exploit constraints beyond the Shannon inequalities.

item.title: HELLO, GOODBYE: Concurrent General Composition From Super-Rushing Security
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2651
Authors: Anirudh Chandramouli
Summary: Kushilevitz, Lindell, and Rabin (STOC `06, SIAM Journal on Computing `10), in their seminal result, showed that any standalone-secure synchronous multiparty computation (MPC) protocol can be compiled into one secure under concurrent general composition, by adding a synchronisation step after every round; thereby, at least doubling the round complexity. We show that for protocols that are secure against super-rushing adversaries, introduced by Asharov, Chandramouli, Cohen, and Ishai (EuroCrypt `25), two synchronisation rounds suffice. Specifically, for an $R$-round protocol that is secure against super-rushing adversaries with a black-box, straight-line simulator, adding a round of start synchronisation (saying ``HELLO'') and a round of end synchronisation (saying ``GOODBYE'') yields security under concurrent general composition with selective abort in $R+2$ rounds. If the end synchronisation is over a broadcast channel, the security is upgraded to unanimous abort. Both compilers incur no loss in the security reduction and preserve the flavour of security (perfect, statistical, or computational) of the underlying synchronous protocol. Moreover, combining with the sufficient conditions of Asharov et al. for perfect security, and the round-preserving super-rushing compilers of Ciampi, Ravi, and Zou (Cryptology ePrint Archive 2026/1745) for statistical and computational security, yields compilers from rushing security to security under concurrent general composition, with an additive overhead of at most $2$ rounds.
We further extend our compilers to protocols with a trusted setup, such as a common reference string or a public-key infrastructure, which is necessary in the dishonest majority setting. We require two conditions. First, every execution of the protocol uses its own stateless copy of the setup, whose responses to the adversary do not depend on the interactions of the honest parties. In particular, this rules out setups that are shared across executions, such as a global common reference string or a single public-key infrastructure used by every execution. Second, the underlying protocol is secure against super-rushing adversaries with adaptive inputs, that is, even when the inputs are chosen after interacting with the setup. Under these conditions, the same compilers yield security under concurrent general composition. We also show that adaptive inputs cannot be relaxed to the usual notion of security in the setup-hybrid model. Specifically, we give a protocol that is statistically secure against super-rushing adversaries with guaranteed output delivery under the standard hybrid model, but is insecure under concurrent general composition after adding start and end synchronisation, even with selective abort.

item.title: On Robust Combiners for Pseudorandom Codes and PKE with Pseudorandom Ciphertexts
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2650
Authors: Nico Döttling, Venkata Koppula, Mahesh Sreekumar Rajasree, Felix Rohrbach
Summary: Robust combiners are a standard way to hedge cryptographic assumptions: given several candidate constructions, they produce one construction that remains secure as long as one candidate is secure. In favorable cases, such combiners also yield universal constructions. We ask whether this paradigm applies to cryptographic primitives whose public outputs must be both pseudorandom and sparse.
Our first result gives a negative answer for pseudorandom codes (PRCs), i.e., error-correcting codes whose codewords are computationally indistinguishable from uniform strings. We prove that secret-key PRCs admit no black-box robust combiner. The impossibility holds even for the weakest meaningful guarantee, where the combined scheme is required to be secure when all but one candidate PRC are secure.
We then show that the obstruction is not specific to error correction. In the sparse ciphertext regime, public-key encryption with pseudorandom ciphertexts also admits no black-box robust combiner. This stands in contrast to ordinary IND-CPA encryption, for which robust combiners are easy to obtain. Thus the requirement that public outputs look uniformly random introduces a genuine barrier to black-box assumption hedging, and rules out the standard combiner route to universal constructions for these primitives.

item.title: LINE-Break: Cryptanalysis and Reverse Engineering of Letter Sealing
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2649
Authors: Diego F. Aranha, Adam Blatchley Hansen, Thomas Kingo T. Mogensen
Summary: We present a security analysis of the messaging service known as LINE, a popular platform used daily by millions of users in East and Southeast Asia – most notably Japan, Taiwan, Thailand, and Indonesia. More specifically, we focus on its underlying custom end-to-end encryption (E2EE) protocol, known as Letter Sealing v2. Our findings show that Letter Sealing allows a TLS Machine-in-the- Middle attacker or malicious server to violate integrity, authenticity, and confidentiality of communications. The stateless design of the protocol allows message replay, reordering, and blocking attacks without the user being notified. The lack of origin authentication facilitates impersonation attacks, in which the authorship of mes- sages in one-to-one or group chats can be forged by malicious users colluding with the adversary. Lastly, stickers and URL previews present a notable leakage of plaintext, which leads to a violation of confidentiality. To verify the correctness of our findings, we mounted a Machine-in-the-Middle attack on an iOS device, yielding the device’s outgoing traffic and the corresponding server responses. Utilizing this setup, we experimentally verified our attacks against the authentic LINE application and an independent implementation. We discuss our findings in comparison to the state-of-the-art E2EE protocols, and conclude that Letter Sealing does not satisfy the requirements expected from a modern E2EE messaging protocol.

item.title: Notes on BulletProofs++ Range Proofs
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2648
Authors: Philipp Jovanovic, Arnab Roy
Summary: We review the Bulletproofs++ construction which replaces the bit-decomposition inner-product argument of Bulletproofs with a reciprocal set-membership argument over base-$16$ digits. We present a self-contained specification of the $64$-bit range proof as well as a general batched variant parametric in the batch size $M$ and bit width $b$ and prove honest-verifier zero-knowledge and exact-form knowledge soundness. We describe the evaluation and optimizations of our Rust implementation over Ristretto255, which proves up to $7.8\times$ and verifies up to $4.5\times$ faster than regular Bulletproofs. Finally, we correct two formulas of the original paper: the affine $T^3$ term of the scalar polynomial $p_s(T)$ carries a factor of $2$, and the slot-$0$ component of the blinding vector $r_S$ carries the opposite sign.

item.title: Revisiting ZMAC+: Birthday-Bound Attacks and a Beyond-Birthday-Bound Repair
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2647
Authors: Yan Jia, Peng Wang, Lei Hu, Shuping Mao, Tingting Guo, Jiadong Han
Summary: ZMAC+ is a tweakable-block-cipher-based MAC proposed by List and Nandi in ToSC 2017 with claimed beyond-birthday-bound security. We show that a tag-swap mechanism previously observed for a hypothetical two-output extension of DoveMAC also applies to the published ZMAC+ construction. For two-block tags, we give a distinguisher with constant advantage and a fresh-message forgery with constant success probability using $O(2^{n/2})$ queries in the ideal-TBC model, where $n$ is the block length. An internal collision between two message families exchanges their tag blocks; a common extension preserves this relation and leads to a forgery with one additional authentication query. We identify a counting error in the published Lemma~4 and prove a corrected aggregate differential bound. The resulting PRF and MAC upper bounds match the birthday query threshold for bounded message lengths and two-block tags, under explicit field-order conditions. The distinguisher extends to every legal fixed output length $d\ge2$, and the forgery to every legal even $d$. We also retain ZHash and separate the output domains. Under stated field-order, length, and domain-capacity conditions, this modification admits an adaptive PRF bound of order $q^2/2^{n+\min(n,t)}$ for bounded lengths. Finally, a one-query counterexample shows that the ZAE security theorem must retain the per-message length restriction required by its counter-in-tweak encryption component.

item.title: Mikros: Bitwidth-Aware SNARKs over Extensions of Small Fields
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2646
Authors: Mingshu CONG
Summary: Provers for succinct non-interactive arguments of knowledge (SNARKs) perform arithmetic over a large field for soundness, even when the witness entries are a few bits wide, which inflates both prover time and memory usage. Recent work makes individual SNARK components bitwidth-aware, so that a lower witness bitwidth means faster proving and lower memory usage, but these techniques cover only part of the prover and exploit the structure of specific fields, typically binary ones.
We introduce Mikros, a framework for end-to-end bitwidth-aware SNARK construction based on algebraic vector packing. We pack vectors of length \(N=m\kappa\) over a base field \(\mathbb{F}\) into length-\(m\) vectors over a degree-\(\kappa\) extension field \(\mathbb{E}\), which turns length-\(N\) relations over \(\mathbb{F}\) into length-\(m\) relations over \(\mathbb{E}\) and makes existing linear-time extension-field protocols bitwidth-aware. This technique thus unifies bitwidth-aware inner-product proofs, Hadamard-product proofs, and polynomial commitment schemes, previously obtained by separate constructions, and yields the first bitwidth-aware grand-product proof, hence the first bitwidth-aware permutation argument. Composing them gives bitwidth-aware SNARKs for circuit satisfiability over extensions of arbitrary small fields.
For a single instance of circuit satisfiability, the prover cost is proportional to the effective bitwidth, the combined bitwidth of the witness entries and the wiring-position encodings; across instances of the same circuit, the position encoding is amortized and the per-instance cost is proportional to the witness bitwidth. Although Mikros does not rely on binary-field structure, its prover is \(2.19\times\), \(2.55\times\), and \(1.85\times\) faster on batches of \(256\) SHA-256 compressions, Keccak permutations, and BLAKE3 compressions than Flock (B\"unz \etal, IACR ePrint 2026), the state-of-the-art bitwidth-aware SNARK over binary-extension fields.

item.title: Isotaxis: Optimal Asynchronous Byzantine Consensus with Ordering Linearizability
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2645
Authors: Vincent Gramoli, Zhenliang Lu, Qiang Tang, Pouriya Zarbafian, Xinrui Zhang
Summary: Despite ensuring both consistency and liveness, state machine replication (SMR) protocols remain vulnerable to adversaries that manipulate transaction order, causing, e.g., MEV attacks. To mitigate this, researchers have proposed new variants augmented with order-fairness. However, existing protocols that employ dependency graphs, such as Aequitas (Crypto 2020), Themis (CCS 2023), and SpeedyFair (NDSS 2024), often suffer from suboptimal performance, limited resilience, or weakened security guarantees. Pompē (OSDI 2020) introduced a novel ordering notion called ordering linearizability (OL) that may circumvent those drawbacks. However, its guarantee holds only under favorable network conditions, making the protocol vulnerable to order fairness violations during network delays and susceptible to performance degradation in the presence of Byzantine faults. Also, implementing SMR under OL remains an open challenge in asynchronous settings, as no known protocol achieves this without sacrificing liveness of SMR.
In this paper, we present $\mathsf{Isotaxis}$, a state machine replication with ordering linearizability; moreover, our protocol has communication complexity $\mathcal{O}(n\ell+\lambda n^2)$, where $n$ is the number of processes, $\ell$ is the input (transaction) size, and $\lambda$ is the security parameter. This is optimal when $\ell\geq \lambda n$, while previous works have cubic communication. To the best of our knowledge, $\mathsf{Isotaxis}$ is the first protocol to achieve ordering linearizability in the asynchronous setting, especially one with optimal communication complexity and optimal Byzantine resilience. We implemented $\mathsf{Isotaxis}$ and conducted extensive experiments using up to 100 EC2 c6a.2xlarge instances. The experimental results show that our protocol robustly outperforms Pompē across all system scales, ranging from 4 to 100 nodes.

item.title: Iterated-Logarithmic Additive Hardness for Bin Packing
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2644
Authors: Zhao Song
Summary: The question of obtaining a constant-additive approximation for bin packing was highlighted in the third of ten open problems in Williamson and Shmoys' The Design of Approximation Algorithms [SW11, Chapter~17, Problem~3]. We prove that there is an absolute constant $c>0$ such that, unless $\mathrm P=\mathrm{NP}$, no deterministic polynomial-time packing using at most $\mathrm{OPT}+c\log^*\mathrm{OPT}$ bins, where $\mathrm{OPT}$ is the minimum number of bins. In particular, no such algorithm has additive error $o(\log^*\mathrm{OPT})$.
The best known upper bound, due to Hoberg and Rothvoss [HR17], is $\mathrm{OPT}+O(\log\mathrm{OPT})$, achieved by a randomized algorithm with expected polynomial running time. OpenAI [Ope26] previously showed that, unless $\mathrm P=\mathrm{NP}$, no deterministic polynomial-time algorithm guarantees a packing using at most $\mathrm{OPT}+O(1)$ bins.
We conjecture that the optimal additive approximation error for bin packing is $\Theta(\log \mathrm{OPT})$.

item.title: Non-profiled Single-Trace ML-DSA Secret Key Recovery by Horizontal Distribution Analysis
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2643
Authors: Linus Backlund, Elena Dubrova
Summary: During the last decade, single-trace side-channel attacks on cryptographic implementations have largely focused on profiled methods, which typically assume that the attacker has a clone device and implementation knowledge to build a leakage model for the target before launching the attack. In this paper, we demonstrate that a much weaker adversary, without the ability to profile, can also mount powerful single-trace attacks. The presented method compares the observed sample distribution with the expected Hamming weight leakage distribution using a Gaussian mixture model as a distinguisher. The horizontal nature of the attack allows us to obtain multiple observations per execution by partitioning and stacking the trace. We show how to select optimal parameters for trace preprocessing and configure the measurement setup so that the noise floor is lowered, enabling the exploitation of weak leakage. We also prove that imperfect classifications can be efficiently corrected using information-set decoding algorithms. The new method is evaluated on an optimized implementation of ML-DSA-65 on ARM Cortex-M4 using the secret key unpacking procedure as an attack point. With an enumeration budget of $2^{70}$ operations in $\mathbb Z_q$, the full secret key is recovered from a single trace in 99% of attacks.

item.title: Cryptanalysis and Repair of "Decentralized Multi-authority ABE for NC$^1$ from BDH"
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2642
Authors: Xingwang Wang
Summary: We present a plaintext-recovery attack on both the DBDH-based construction and the CBDH-based variant of Datta, Komargodski, and Waters (Journal of Cryptology, 2023). The attack succeeds with probability one in the claimed static security model using one corrupt authority and two users, each unauthorized even when granted the corrupt authority's attribute. The flaw is an invalid extension of the LSSS matrix-normalization lemma originating with Rouselakis and Waters (FC,~2015): preserving complete-share distributions does not preserve coordinate-wise ciphertext masks, which a corrupt authority can expose to remove identity binding from other users' shares. For both variants, replacing these masks with independent full linear sharings of zero preserves correctness and restores ciphertext-distribution invariance. We prove static security of both repaired variants in the random oracle model under their respective BDH assumptions, using the original hardcore-bit convention for the CBDH variant. Both proofs allow adaptive identity-hash queries. The modification retains the original matrix-width and row-labeling restrictions, keys, decryption, and ciphertext size, requiring only additional encryption randomness and finite-field arithmetic. We also attack both multi-authority attribute-based inner-product functional encryption constructions of Datta and Pal (PKC, 2023) and establish correctness and matrix-substitution invariance of the same repair. We prove static security of the repaired small-universe construction under asymmetric DBDH. For the large-universe construction, we identify a missing source-group encoding in the original reduction and give a complete static security proof under an augmented $L$-DBDH assumption, whose generic bilinear group hardness we establish.

item.title: A Memory-efficient Implementation of Wiedemann XL
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2641
Authors: Daniel Cabarcas, Tung Chou, Felipe Merino, Javier Verbel
Summary: The signature schemes MQOM, SNOVA, MAYO, and UOV are third-round candidates in the NIST standardization process for additional post-quantum signatures, and their security relies on the hardness of the multivariate quadratic (MQ) problem. XL with block Wiedemann (BW) is one of the most efficient MQ solvers in practice, but its memory demand has led to a debate about its memory access cost: generating the rows of the Macaulay matrix on the fly is widely believed to save memory at a non-negligible computational cost.
In this work, we evaluate the memory--time trade-off in practice. We provide the first efficient on-the-fly implementation of XL with BW. We build on the state-of-the-art implementation by Cheng, Chou, Niederhagen, and Yang (CCNY), which uses SSE instructions and supports the fields $\mathbb{F}_2$, $\mathbb{F}_{16}$ and $\mathbb{F}_{31}$; we remove its column-index tables and generate the rows on the fly in the first phase of BW (BW1). We amortize the cost of on-the-fly generation with a new algorithm that computes column indices with $O(n^2)$ instead of $O(n^3)$ table look-ups, where $n$ is the number of variables. In our experiments we observe that our on-the-fly implementation achieves running times comparable to CCNY's with up to five times less memory. We also port both implementations to AVX2 over $\mathbb{F}_{256}$, the main field of UOV, and observe a similar behavior: comparable BW1 running times with less memory for the on-the-fly variant.

item.title: Subexponential Algorithms for LWE via Rejection Sampling on Superlattices
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2640
Authors: Ligeng Fan, Changpeng Shao, Hongbo Li, Dingkang Wang
Summary: Recent superlattice algorithms have improved the provable complexity of lattice problems. Ducas, Engelberts, and Loyer used this framework to obtain a subexponential algorithm for infinity-norm short integer solution, while also identifying a key obstacle to extending it to learning with errors (LWE). A similar difficulty arose in the analysis of Kirchner and Fouque, whose claimed subexponential running time with only linearly many LWE samples was not rigorously established. Building on the framework of Ducas, Engelberts, and Loyer, we develop two refinements based on rejection sampling that solve this open problem.
First, we use rejection sampling to cancel the shift-dependent normalization factor that arises when sampling from a shifted, scaled integer lattice. This factor is a product of one-dimensional Gaussian masses and can be evaluated efficiently. This yields a provably subexponential classical search-LWE algorithm for prime $q\in[n^2,2n^2]$ and constant Gaussian error width. It uses only $m=4n$ independent samples and runs in time and space $\exp(O(n/\ln\ln n))$.
Second, we use random auxiliary superlattices and apply rejection sampling to the difference of two Gaussian lattice samples, ensuring that the accepted output follows the desired discrete Gaussian distribution up to a small statistical error. For $q=n^{\kappa+o(1)}$, $m=n+h=O(n)$, and $R=h\ln q/[m\ln(2+\sigma)]\to\infty$, the resulting algorithm uses time and space $2^{(1/2+o(1))n/\ln R}$, where $\sigma$ is the Gaussian error width. In particular, for $\sigma=n^{o(1)}$ and any fixed $m/n>1$, our algorithm achieves provable subexponential classical running time, whereas the primal and dual baselines have exponential-time bounds and earlier provable subexponential BKW analyses require $\Omega(n\ln n)$ samples.

item.title: Private Information Retrieval with Accountability at Erasure-Optimal Server Redundancy
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2639
Authors: Myeongjun Kim, Hyunseok Jeong, Mincheol Son, Young-Sik Kim
Summary: Private information retrieval (PIR) hides which database item a client requests. We study PIR that also identifies servers that respond incorrectly. Against a coalition of at most $t$ corrupted servers, the client must retrieve the item and identify every deviating server when at most $d$ deviate. Above that threshold, it must abort and return an empty identification set, with a specified statistical error.
We present SynTrace, a single-round compiler for linear PIR supporting audit queries whose honest answers belong to a public code. The client combines the retrieval query with $m$ audit queries using secret linear mixing and independent blinding. Audit syndromes identify deviations before reconstruction. We prove perfect query privacy, zero false-identification probability within the deviation threshold, and statistical realization of an accountable PIR functionality.
For Shamir-based PIR, SynTrace uses $k=t+d+1$ servers. Under the stated privacy and download assumptions, tolerating $d$ missing responses already requires this many servers, so identification adds no server overhead. With this number of servers, $m=d$ audit queries suffice with a suitable field, and are necessary within the specified syndrome-span decoder class. Additional audit queries can reduce communication by allowing a smaller field. For one 32 KiB record from a 1 GiB database, with five servers, privacy and robustness against two corrupted servers, and error at most $2^{-40}$, SynTrace uses 2.25 MiB of communication, compared with 8.96 MiB for the homomorphic-MAC construction of Eriguchi, Kurosawa and Nuida (TCC 2022) under the same workload and thresholds. Batched retrievals can share the audit queries.

item.title: Decision Attacks on Known-Covariance Ring-LWE via Public Gram Determinants
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2638
Authors: Anis Bkakria
Summary: Known-Covariance Ring-LWE (KCov-RLWE) was introduced by Micciancio and Suhl to support simulation-secure threshold encryption. It strengthens ordinary Ring-LWE by revealing an exact quadratic summary of the hidden secret and errors, and its decisional hardness was left open.
We give explicit polynomial-time decision attacks for broad families of prime moduli at ring rank one. Our key observation is that the public sample and the covariance hint together determine a bordered Gram matrix whose determinant exposes a hidden residual with a different distribution for genuine and uniform samples. After reducing the ring into finite-field components, this residual has one of two forms: a product across reciprocal components, or a Hermitian norm when a component is preserved by conjugation. The latter case yields a particularly strong distinguishing signal. Moreover, reduction modulo any divisor preserves the KCov real and random experiments exactly, so every attackable odd prime divisor of a composite modulus transfers the corresponding distinguisher with no loss of advantage.
The attack covers the one-sample setting globally in the self-reciprocal regime and, under the coefficient-product Gaussian specialization, locally in the completely split regime. More generally, we obtain a complete classification of how this residual-based attack behaves for odd prime moduli when $m\ge2$, and extend these guarantees to arbitrary moduli possessing a suitable odd prime divisor. The classification does not imply insecurity for every parameter family: when the relevant residue fields are sufficiently large, the guaranteed distinguishing advantage in the reciprocal case can become negligible, and pure power-of-two moduli remain outside the divisor-reduction extension. Accordingly, our results invalidate the KCov pseudorandomness assumption in the quantified families; they do not show that every parameter choice permitted by the motivating Ring-PKE sketch is insecure, nor do they give a direct IND-CPA break of the complete threshold-encryption construction.

item.title: Maximum-Likelihood Decoding of Gabidulin Codes Is NP-Hard Even in Dimension One
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2637
Authors: Philippe Gaborit
Summary: Fix a prime power q . We prove that deciding whether a received word y ∈ F^n_qm lies at rank distance at most n − 2 from the one-dimensional Gabidulin code {λg : λ in Fqm } is NP-complete. Thus maximum-likelihood decoding of Gabidulin codes is NP-hard even for k = 1, an analogue of the Guruswami-Vardy theorem for Reed-Solomon codes. In the Hamming metric, by contrast, hardness at this radius requires the dimension to grow with the length, as in the Guruswami Vardy theorem. The reduction is deterministic; consequently Rank Syndrome Decoding (RSD) and Rank Minimum Distance (RMD) for Fqm -linear codes are NP-complete under deterministic polynomial reductions, whereas the previously known reduction was randomized. The proof goes through a pivot problem that we introduce, Twisted Square Membership (TSM): given Fq -subspaces U, W in FqN , decide whether some non-zero a ∈ U satisfies a^(q+1) in W . Quadratic systems in d unknowns are encoded into TSM, then TSM into Gabidulin decoding. The last step views the received word as an Fq -linear map and decoding at radius n − 2 as the search for an Fq -plane on which it acts as a scalar. With support U + τ W in a cubic extension and map a + τ b → a^(q^2) + τ b^q , two Frobenius twists force solution planes to encode the relation a^(q+1) ∈ W . All constructions are explicit and polynomial, with N = O(qd^2 ), n ≤ N + d, and m = 3N .

item.title: Revisiting AES Key Wrap: Forgery Bounds, Structural Observations, and Recommendations for the Revision of NIST SP 800-38F
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2636
Authors: John Preuß Mattsson
Summary: NIST is revising SP~800-38F, which specifies the AES Key Wrap modes KW and KWP. This paper is an updated and expanded version of our technical comments to NIST. We show that the forgery probabilities stated in SP~800-38F do not account for adaptive attacks, give the resulting forgery probabilities for KW, KWP, and TKW, and show that checking the expected plaintext length can raise the security level of KWP considerably. Revisiting Kelsey's long-message observation, we correct the collision conditions, show that a successful forgery leaks a plaintext prefix, derive an encryption-only distinguisher, and conclude that KW does not have beyond-birthday-bound security. We explain the role of the step counter, analyse the single-semiblock path of KWP and the trade-off between the number of passes and the length limit, and give recommendations for the revision, for implementations, and for future key-wrap designs.

item.title: A Kelsey–Kohno Attack Variant against SHA-2 Message Digests in HSS/LMS and XMSS
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2635
Authors: Falko Strenzke
Summary: We present a multi-target second-preimage attack on the message hashing of the stateful hash-based signature schemes HSS/LMS and XMSS with SHA-256 and with the truncated SHA-256/192. The attack builds on the herding technique of Kelsey and Kohno: the attacker takes the chaining states that follow the per-signature prefixes of many collected signatures and merges them, level by level through state collisions, into a single chaining state. From that state one search serves all collected signatures at once, which defeats the commitment to the key and to the one-time-signature leaf index at the start of the hash input that is meant to rule out multi-target attacks. The search can match the final digests, which is the better choice against SHA-256/192, or, after appending a Kelsey-Schneier expandable message, the internal chaining states of long signed messages, which is effective for full SHA-256. For SHA-256 with NIST's bound of $2^{64}$ signatures, which may be spread over any number of keys, the cost in compression-function calls falls from the nominal $2^{256}$ to about $2^{166}$ for messages of up to 4 GiB and to about $2^{156}$ in the formal limit of maximal message length, a loss of 100 bits. For SHA-256/192, digest matching costs about $2^{153}$ for $2^{64}$ signatures of any length, a loss of 39 bits. Because the attack pools signatures across keys, even the first signature of an individual key contributes to a potential overall exposure of an ecosystem. The attacks exploit the chaining state of SHA-256, which is narrower than twice the targeted security level; the SHAKE256 parameter sets are not affected.

item.title: Nearly Optimal Hardness for CVP and NCP with Preprocessing
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2634
Authors: Giacomo Fenzi, Guy Weissenberg
Summary: The closest vector problem(CVP)and the nearest codeword problem (NCP) are fundamental computational problems with connections to learning, coding theory, and cryptography. We study hardness of approximation in the preprocessing model: an algorithm receives the lattice or code in advance, may perform unrestricted computation to produce polynomial-size advice, and must then solve the problem on any target in polynomial time. Unless $\mathsf{NP} \subseteq \mathsf{P/poly}$, no such algorithm achieves an approximation factor of $\bullet$ $M^{1−\varepsilon}$ for NCP over any fixed finite field, or $\bullet$ $M^{1/\min\{p,2\}−\varepsilon}$ for CVP in any $\ell_p$ norm, for every fixed $\varepsilon > 0$, where $M$ denotes the code block length or lattice dimension, respectively. We improve the subpolynomial factors of Khot, Popat, and Vishnoi [KPV14]to polynomial ones, matching the exponents that Song [Son26] proved without preprocessing for binary codes and the $\ell_2$ norm. We further extend Song’s evaluation tables to every fixed prime characteristic and the lattice reduction to $\ell_p$ with $p > 2$. Our main technical contribution is an extension of the moment method, introduced in an OpenAI report [Ope26] and improved by Song [Son26], to the preprocessing setting. In addition, we give a direct reduction from probabilistically checkable proofs (PCPs) whose query locations and families of possible predicates do not depend on the formula. The resulting factor of $M^{\Omega(1/(\log \log M)^2)}$ is already larger than that of [KPV14], and the reduction may be of independent interest.

item.title: On the Inapplicability of Residue-Confined Error Attacks to CRT-FHE with Non-Degenerate Error Distributions
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2633
Authors: Anil Kumar Pradhan, Abhraneel Dutta
Summary: This paper responds to the cryptanalysis presented in “Key Recovery from Residue- Confined Errors in the Pradhan CRT-RLWE Construction” (Olejnik and Naskrecki, 2026), which claims key recovery and plaintext recovery against the CRT-FHE scheme introduced in “A New CRT-based Fully Homomorphic Encryption” (Pradhan et al., 2026).
We demonstrate that the reported recovery attacks rely entirely on a deliberately con- structed error distribution whose support lies in the kernel of the CRT encoding function. Consequently, the effective encryption error is identically zero, reducing the attacked con- struction to a noiseless RLWE instance. The subsequent key-recovery and plaintext-recovery results therefore follow from the deliberate elimination of the encryption noise, rather than from any cryptanalytic method capable of recovering secrets from properly noise-bearing CRT-FHE ciphertexts.
Crucially, the proposed attack neither removes nor estimates errors from normally generated CRT-FHE ciphertexts. Instead, it assumes an artificial error distribution specifically chosen to guarantee their annihilation during encoding. This condition does not hold for the intended centered-binomial error distribution, under which the probability that an entire error polynomial belongs to the encoder’s kernel is negligible at the reported parameters. Thus, the presented recovery procedures do not constitute attacks against the concrete CRT-FHE instantiation with its intended non-degenerate error distribution.
We conclude that the reported key-recovery and plaintext-recovery results concern a deliberately degenerate, effectively zero-error instantiation and do not demonstrate a practical security compromise of CRT-FHE under its intended error sampling.
We further show that the distributional mismatch identified in the claimed RLWE hardness reduction does not constitute a cryptanalytic attack. In fact, the CRT-encoded error distribution under the intended parameters admits an exact, invertible transformation to ordinary RLWE with an explicitly characterized non-degenerate ternary error law.

item.title: Chosen Commitments and Certified Decoding Regions in the Adaptive Threshold Schnorr Attack
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2632
Authors: Hüseyin Eren Demirtaş, Oğuz Yayla
Summary: Crites and Stewart reduce an adaptive forgery attack on threshold Schnorr signatures with $N$ parties and threshold $\tau$ to one call to a sparse linear search oracle, which they show to be bounded distance decoding of a diagonally scaled Reed–Solomon code and whose sparse answer, a witness, names the parties to corrupt. Their analysis samples the coefficient vector behind the adversary's commitment uniformly at random and leaves open whether a chosen vector does better. We bound the success of an adversary that follows their template with a chosen vector and recovers witnesses only inside regions built from the radii that seven decoding theorems, three for Reed–Solomon and four for folded Reed–Solomon codes, certify under their own setup hypotheses. When the commitment is fixed through a known coefficient vector before a fresh hash challenge, the attack target is, conditional on the history that fixed the vector, a uniform point of a line. For distinct nonzero Shamir points, our main theorem shows that every such line contains at most $M$ targets with a witness in a finite collection of coordinate and block weight regions fixed before the targets, each permitting fewer than $\tau$ nonzero coordinates, for an explicit integer $M$ depending only on $N$, $\tau$ and the collection. We call the adversary the wrapper when it makes at most $Q$ fresh challenges and no signing query, chooses each coefficient vector from its history before the challenge and keeps it afterwards, and lets its solvers make no further signature hash queries. It accepts only a witness of the same target and representation that lies in the regions of the collection within its corruption cap, corrupts parties only once it holds such a witness, and then forges from that witness and stops. Hence the wrapper succeeds with probability at most $QM/p$, with $p$ the group order, even if its solvers recover every witness in the regions at no cost. On the six pairs $(N,\tau)$ of the original attack, fixed collections built from partitions into consecutive blocks contain all seven certified regions and have $M$ below $2^{24}$, so at the field size proxy $p = 2^{252}$ the bound stays below $2^{-100}$ after $2^{128}$ challenges. For uniform targets we prove much smaller bounds on the witness probability in these regions. For the folded Guruswami–Wang and Ashvinkumar–Habib–Srivastava block regions on partitions into consecutive blocks fixed before the target, this probability is negligible for polynomially many parties, exponentially large fields and $\tau/N$ bounded away from zero. These results also classify the studied decoder theorems. The hardness of the oracle, the success of other strategies and the adaptive security of threshold Schnorr schemes are open.

item.title: On the Subtleties of Non-Malleability in IVC: Notions, Attacks and Constructions from Falsifiable Assumptions
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2631
Authors: Matteo Campanelli, Suvradip Chakraborty, Chaya Ganesh
Summary: We investigate non-malleable Incrementally Verifiable Computation (IVC), a subject that has received limited attention. We focus on whether and how simulation-sound IVC can be obtained from falsifiable assumptions. We provide additional evidence of the unique aspects of non-malleable incremental proofs, identifying definitional challenges in formalizing simulation-sound IVC, and showing how existing IVC designs from falsifiable assumptions cannot exhibit simulation-soundness "for free" (without modifications). In addition to a new family of definitions of simulation-sound IVC, our main results are the following.
- A general negative result: common Valiant-style proofs are malleable. We isolate and formalize a feature shared by the dominant Valiant-style IVC designs (Valiant, TCC 2008) related to the ability to merge proofs together. We show that, assuming one-way functions, natural zero-knowledge versions of Valiant's design are malleable. As an implication of our framework of attacks, we show that the only IVC for NP from falsifiable assumptions (Datta et al., CRYPTO 2025) cannot satisfy any form of simulation-soundness; this is the case even when instantiating this scheme from non-malleable building blocks.
- A positive result: first IVC from falsifiable assumptions with non-malleability features. We construct an IVC satisfying a non-trivial form of simulation-soundness under subexponential iO and either subexponential LWE or subexponential bilinear-map assumptions.

item.title: Exact Error Bootstrapping and Comb Bootstrapping in FHEW/TFHE
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2630
Authors: Philippe Chartier, Mohammed Lemou
Summary: In FHEW and TFHE, bootstrapping evaluates the decryption function via a blind rotation, whose resolution limits the message space. We propose instead to bootstrap the \emph{error}. By rounding the ciphertext at a resolution that is a multiple of the message modulus, we preserve the message exactly. Reduction modulo a small integer then yields a noise-free encryption of the error, which a single blind rotation lifts exactly before it is subtracted. The message modulus is thus constrained solely by the noise and can be much larger than in standard TFHE. Since the error takes far fewer distinct values than the ring degree, a single blind rotation can also refresh several ciphertexts simultaneously. We call this procedure the comb bootstrap. Between refreshes, an integer remains encrypted in a single ciphertext, allowing additions modulo the message modulus and multiplications without programmable bootstrapping. Built on TFHE-rs, for $8$-bit integers on a single thread, our refresh is $3.5$ times faster than that of TFHE-rs, and $9.1$ times faster with the comb bootstrap; multiplication is $6.5$ times faster. In a residue number system, multiplication of integers modulo $\widehat P\ge 2^{32}$ is $19$ times faster than in TFHE-rs. The error bootstrap serves exclusively to refresh ciphertexts; evaluating any other function still requires programmable bootstrapping.

item.title: VeilDNS: Post-Quantum DNS Privacy from the First UDP Packet
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2629
Authors: Aditya Singh Rawat, Mahabir Prasad Jhanwar, Rei Safavi-Naini
Summary: DNS was designed around UDP, and most DNS traffic today still follows that design: one query, one response, and no handshake. This makes DNS fast and scalable, but exposes client queries in cleartext. DoT, DoH, and DoQ provide privacy by encrypting DNS messages with TLS. This works once TLS/TCP or QUIC handshakes complete, but cold sessions spend extra round trips and CPU before the first private query can be sent—a cost that grows with post-quantum cryptography.
We present VeilDNS, a DNS-native protocol that uses a post-quantum KEM and AEAD to encrypt DNS questions and answers and authenticate the resolver in a single UDP exchange. Given an authenticated resolver KEM key, clients have query privacy from their first UDP packet. VeilDNS supports stateless and stateful modes—the latter reducing recurring computation and bandwidth. An optional mode provides forward secrecy from the second query onward. By preserving the DNS wire format, VeilDNS runs on the standard UDP port 53.
Compared with ML-DSA-authenticated Do(T/H/Q) on the well-provisioned network profile, VeilDNS's stateless and stateful modes achieve up to $3.5\times$ higher cold-session throughput, $4.8\times$ lower average latency, $4.7\times$ lower CPU time, $13.7\times$ fewer bytes, and $15.8\times$ fewer packets. On the constrained profile, the throughput gain reaches $12.4\times$. Tamarin establishes query confidentiality, response authentication, and forward secrecy.

item.title: Extraction meets Distillation - cryptanalytic techniques to recover parameters from a Deep Neural Network
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2628
Authors: Biprarshi Biswas, Arya Anshuman Ojha, Yubaraj Das, Devansh Khosla, Kamran Rais, Saankhya Samanta, Subhamoy Maitra, Pantelimon Stanica
Summary: We study fully connected neural-network reconstruction by combining cryptanalytic weight-direction extraction with learning from predicted labels. We adapt a ReLU extraction implementation to Leaky ReLU, compare sign-search methods, and estimate biases and output layers. We prove conditional bounds for direction recovery with approximate prefixes, preservation of local distance votes, prediction changes from aligned parameter errors, and sign selection with independent scoring data. We also specify exact row restoration and distinguish its guarantee from that of gradient masking. The experiments evaluate assisted extraction, with privileged access to gradients, hidden activations, and victim parameters, followed by label-based reconstruction. Across eight search seeds on the largest synthetic architecture, Leaky ReLU recovers 51--57 neurons in the deepest hidden layer, while ReLU recovers none. This advantage does not hold uniformly across architectures and layers. Removing victim-weight access from the sign walk gives less accurate signs, despite high final prediction agreement. Across 40 seeded runs on the two smallest synthetic victims, agreement on 5,000 inputs excluded from fitting and selection ranges from $0.9890$ to $0.9992$. On two CIFAR-10 victims, the reconstructed models achieve $56.40\%$ and $58.29\%$ agreement and exceed the distillation baseline on three functional metrics. We report label requests separately from privileged access and explain why prediction agreement does not identify network parameters.

item.title: Strongly Adaptive Asynchronous Byzantine Agreement with Linear Communication and Almost-Everywhere Termination
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2627
Authors: Renas Bacho, Simon Holmgaard Kamp, Julian Loss, Jesper Buus Nielsen, Maciej Obremski
Summary: It is well known that Byzantine agreement requires $\Omega(t^2)$ messages against a strongly adaptive adversary that may corrupt $t=\Theta(n)$ parties and suppress a party's undelivered messages upon corruption. We circumvent this lower bound by relaxing termination: for any constant $0<\nu<1$, at least a $(1-\nu)$ fraction of the honest parties terminate, while agreement and validity hold for every honest decision. For every constant corruption gap $\delta>0$ and every $t\leq(1-\delta)n/3$, we construct binary agreement with this guarantee in authenticated asynchronous networks against strongly adaptive corruptions with message takebacks. Except with negligible probability, these guarantees hold and every honest decision carries a transferable justifier. The protocol achieves almost-everywhere termination in expected $O(1)$ rounds, expected total communication $O(n\kappa^2)$ bits, and expected maximum communication $\widetilde O(\kappa^2)$ bits over honest parties before corruption, where $\kappa$ is the computational security parameter.
Our construction combines a recursively shared BLS signing key with certificate dissemination over a sparse graph. The recursive sharing is used to implement threshold signing with distinct safety and liveness thresholds. Dissemination propagates existing certificates to almost all honest parties. The construction uses a trusted setup and is secure in the random oracle model under the algebraic one-more computational Diffie--Hellman assumption.
We further obtain full binary agreement with the same asymptotic communication and round complexity against adaptive corruptions without message takebacks. The extension requires neither atomic multi-send nor private communication channels.

item.title: The Exact Bit Security of Hash-Based Signatures
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2626
Authors: Mikhail Kudinov, Benedikt Wagner, Emile Wambsgans
Summary: In this work, we analyze the security of hash-based signatures in Lean4. We examine how different ways of accounting for an adversary’s work yield different notions of bit security. As our working example, we study two instances of XMSS with $128$ bit digests.
Under most of the accounting modes we consider, we get $127$ bit security for strong unforgeability. However, under the most conservative convention that counts only the adversary’s direct random oracle queries, we only get $122$ bits of security. We prove these bounds in the random oracle model without computational hardness assumptions and give matching attacks. We also prove a tight bound of $127$ bits of strong unforgeability for SLH-DSA-128s.
Our work is primarily motivated by recent autoresearch competitions, and it demonstrates the concrete impact of resource accounting. We hope that it helps designers of future challenges make an informed decision when choosing a notion of bit security that reflects their needs.

item.title: Faster Polynomial Factorization over Finite Fields via Batched Modular Composition
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2625
Authors: Zhenyu Xiong, Mingsheng Wang
Summary: In the algebraic model, where one counts operations in $\mathbb{F}_q$ uniformly in the characteristic, the best published algorithm for factoring a polynomial of degree $n$ over $\mathbb{F}_q$, due to Kaltofen and Shoup with the rectangular products of Huang and Pan, uses $n^{1.80535+o(1)}\log q$ operations, and its bottleneck is the modular compositions of the giant steps. A new algorithm is presented for these compositions. Like the algorithm of Neiger, Salvy, Schost and Villard, the new method is based on the relation matrices of the argument. Since all compositions at one level of the giant steps share one argument, the relation matrices and a table of remainders are computed only once, and the remaining work consists of rectangular matrix products. For the two-matrix evaluation, we prove that a random change of basis puts every Frobenius image in good position. This reduces the cost of factorization in this model $$\text{from}\quad n^{1.80535+o(1)}\log q\quad\text{to}\quad n^{1.5532+o(1)}\log q,$$ and to $n^{3/2+o(1)}\log q$ if $\omega=2$; with the compositions of Neiger, Salvy, Schost and Villard performed one at a time, the exponent would be $1.7147$. In the bit model, and algebraically in small characteristic, Kedlaya and Umans obtained the exponent $3/2$. For a single composition with an arbitrary argument modulo a separable polynomial, the content of one short relation separates large value fibers, which gives a Las Vegas algorithm for every input at the exponent $(\omega+3)/4<1.3429$, previously known only for generic inputs, and a fourth evaluation level, with truncated powers obtained by transposition, lowers it to $1.3309$. As applications, we obtain faster algorithms for normal bases, minimal polynomials and irreducibility testing, and, for large $q$, factorization in $O(n^{1.5983})+n^{1+o(1)}\log q$ operations.

item.title: Provable Security of SHA-256-Based LMS Revisited in the Ideal-Cipher Model
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2624
Authors: Chun Guo, Hao Cheng, Bart Preneel, Meiqin Wang
Summary: The hash-based Leighton-Micali Signature (LMS) has been standardized by IETF, NIST and ISO. State-of-the-art non-quantum security proofs for LMS have been given by Katz (SSR 2016) and Fluhrer (Eprint 2017/553). However, the actual structure of SHA-256(/192) is the (chopped) Merkle-Damg{\aa}rd construction using a blockcipher-based Davies-Meyer function, and precise security bounds of SHA-256-based LMS\_SHA256\_M32 and SHA-256/192-based LMS\_SHA256\_M24 should be derived in the {\it ideal-cipher model (ICM)}. This was {\it not} considered in Katz and Fluhrer's proofs. In fact, by leveraging structural properties of (chopped) Merkle-Damg{\aa}rd, we exhibit forgery attacks against LMS\_SHA256\_M32 and LMS\_SHA256\_M24 that expose the inapplicability of Katz's and Fluhrer's random-oracle bounds to the concrete SHA-256 constructions. The precise security guarantees of LMS\_SHA256\_M32 and LMS\_SHA256\_M24 thus remain unknown (and are also missing in the standards).
To bridge the structural gap, we provide ICM-based security proofs for the additive-Davies-Meyer abstractions of LMS\_SHA256\_M32 and LMS\_SHA256\_M24. The security level of LMS\_SHA256\_M32 is roughly $256-\log_2 \widehat{B}$ bits, where $\widehat{B}$ is the number of blocks in SHA-256 calls internally made by LMS\_SHA256\_M32 and $\widehat{B}\ll2^{128}$. The security level of LMS\_SHA256\_M24 is roughly $\min \{ 192 - \log_2 \widehat{\Gamma} , 256-\log_2 \widehat{B} \}$ bits, where $\widehat{\Gamma}$ is the number of SHA-256/192 calls internally made by LMS\_SHA256\_M24 and $\widehat{B}$ is the number of blocks in them, and $\widehat{B}\ll2^{128}$ and $\widehat{B} \widehat{\Gamma} \ll 2^{192}$. In conclusion, LMS\_SHA256\_M32 and LMS\_SHA256\_M24 ensure a moderate (yet not ``full'') level of security.

item.title: The Covering Radius of $\operatorname{RM}(2,8)$ is Between $88$ and $91$
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2623
Authors: Xiang-dong Hou, Evelyn Sabo, Freeman Slaughter
Summary: Let $\operatorname{RM}(r,n)$ be the $r$th order Reed--Muller code of length $2^n$, and let $\rho(r,n)$ denote its covering radius. The values $\rho(2,6)=18$ and $\rho(2,7)=40$ are known, whereas the exact value of $\rho(2,8)$ remains open. Starting from the current state of the art bound $88\leq\rho(2,8)\leq96$, we give a computer-assisted reduction of the upper bound $\rho(2,8)\leq91$. We first show that every even-weight Boolean function on eight variables is within distance $90$ of a quadratic function. Changing one value then gives the bound $91$ for odd-weight functions. Our main lemma addresses rank-four seven-variable quintics: when their second-order distance is $36$ and their maximum quadratic-shift first-order distance is $56$, they have at least $60$ minimizing quadratic cosets and at most $12$ cosets of cost $56$. The complete proof covers all $68443$ quartic classes. For every rank-four quintic, the distance-$56$ cosets are enumerated outright, and the $5199$ words are examined individually. Profile counts, hyperplane contractions, and support moments then give the even-weight bound. We describe the calculations and enumerations, together with the classification upon which the proof depends. Instructions to verify the computer search portion may be found at $\texttt{https://github.com/EvelynSabo/RM28}$.

item.title: Faster Matrix Multiplication Leads to Faster Lattice Sieving
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2622
Authors: Yiming Gao, Honggang Hu
Summary: Let $\omega$ denote the matrix multiplication exponent. Very recently, OpenAI showed that $\omega\le9/4$. We demonstrate that, for any fixed $\eta>0$, if $\omega\le9/4-\eta$, then there is a constant $\delta=\delta(\eta)>0$ such that heuristic lattice sieving can be improved to $(3/2-\delta)^{n/2+o(n)}$ time under the spherical heuristic used in the BDGL analysis. With known matrix multiplication algorithms, our method already yields subquadratic search within BDGL buckets.

item.title: Bounds on polynomial approximations of the discrete logarithm function
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2621
Authors: Swastik Kopparty, Rishabh Kothary, Ashutosh Shankar
Summary: We revisit a classical result of Coppersmith and Shparlinski [CS00] showing bounds on how well polynomials can approximate the discrete log function. They showed that for any univariate polynomial $f(X) \in \mathbb{F}_p[X]$ with $\deg(f) \leq D$, we have: $$ |\{ x \in \mathbb{F}_p^\times \mid f(x) = \mathsf{dlog}(x) \}| \leq \sqrt{2 D p}.$$ We show two improvements:
(1) For all $D$, we improve the upper bound above to $(1+o(1)) \cdot \sqrt{Dp}$. In particular, we give nontrivial upper bounds on the approximation even for $D > p/2$. This new upper bound is the Johnson bound from the theory of list-decoding of error-correcting codes, and in fact our proof uses a connection to that problem, as well as other combinatorial ideas.
(2) For $D = 1$, where both the above bounds are $\mathcal{O}(\sqrt{p})$, we give an asymptotically improved upper bound of $\mathcal{O}(p^{2/5})$. This is based on the sum-product phenomenon of additive combinatorics.
We also improve the [CS00] bounds on the number of points of the form $(x, \mathsf{dlog}(x)) \in \mathbb{F}_p^2$ that any bivariate polynomial $Q(X,Y) \in \mathbb{F}_p[X,Y]$ with $\deg(Q) \leq D$ can vanish on, with our new bounds approaching the analogue of the Johnson bound for this problem.

item.title: When Elliptic-Curve Semiprimality Certificates Reveal Factors
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2620
